extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of English constitutional and parliamentary law (lawyers, judges, legislators, legal historians)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of the laws and customs of the UK Parliament (House of Lords and House of Commons), with detailed rules on privileges, elections (qualifications, disqualifications, procedures, anti-corruption measures), and the legislative process (bill stages, royal assent, adjournment/prorogation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer forest privilege
rubrics_metrics.description: Every lord spiritual or temporal summoned to parliament, passing through the king's forests, may, both in going and returning, kill one or two of the king's deer without warrant; in view of the forester, if he be present; or on blowing a horn if he be absent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Declared by the charter of the forest and confirmed in parliament 9 Hen. III; a specific ancient personal privilege of peers with procedural conditions to avoid stealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of peers to legal attendance
rubrics_metrics.description: Peers have a right to be attended by the judges of the court of king's bench and common pleas, such barons of the exchequer as are of the coif, masters of chancery, secretaries of state, the attorney and solicitor general, and the king's learned counsel (serjeants).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attendance is for legal advice and dignity of proceedings; practice has varied as some of these officers have been members of Commons and attendance has fallen into disuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer proxy voting by royal licence
rubrics_metrics.description: Every peer, by licence obtained from the king, may make another lord of parliament his proxy, to vote for him in his absence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a privilege peculiar to peers and is not available to members of the other house, who are proxies for their constituents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of peers to enter dissent (protest)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each peer has a right, by leave of the house, when a vote passes contrary to his sentiments, to enter his dissent on the journals of the house, with the reasons for such dissent (styled his protest).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must be entered with leave of the house; usual practice to record reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of bills affecting peerage
rubrics_metrics.description: All bills that may in their consequences any way affect the rights of the peerage are by the custom of parliament to have their first rise and beginning in the house of peers, and to suffer no changes or amendments in the house of commons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Customary rule protecting peerage rights from alteration by Commons; implies exclusivity of origination and protection against amendment in Commons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative peers statute (6 Ann. c. 23)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statute regulating the election of the sixteen representative peers of North Britain, prescribing the oaths, mode of balloting, prohibiting unusual attendance, and providing that no other matter shall be treated of in that assembly except the election, on pain of praemunire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific statutory procedure for Scottish representative peers following the Union; emphasizes limited agenda and penal sanction for deviation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commons' exclusive right to originate supplies (money bills)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the ancient indisputable privilege and right of the house of commons that all grants of subsidies or parliamentary aids do begin in their house, and are first bestowed by them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason given is that supplies are raised upon the people; thus money bills (all bills directing money to be raised on the subject for any purpose) begin in Commons, and Lords are limited to rejection rather than amendment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and scope of 'money bill'
rubrics_metrics.description: Money bills include all bills by which money is directed to be raised upon the subject, for any purpose or in any shape whatsoever; either for exigencies of government collected from the kingdom in general, as the land tax; or for private benefit and collected in any particular district, as by turnpikes, parish rates, and the like.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This broad definition is used to justify Commons' exclusive origination and to constrain Lords' power to amend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential Lords' alteration exception (Hale)
rubrics_metrics.description: Case noted by Sir Matthew Hale: if commons grant a tax for four years and lords alter it to a less time (e.g., two years), the alteration may be consistent with the grant and need not be sent back to the commons for concurrence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as a narrow, historically founded exception that is unlikely to be repeated under the modern idea of Commons' privilege.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three electoral safeguards (overview)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws guard against usurpation or abuse of the power of choosing representatives by provisions reducible to three points: (1) the qualifications of the electors, (2) the qualifications of the elected, (3) the proceedings at elections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framework for the detailed statutory and customary rules that follow; emphasizes importance of regulating suffrage in a representative system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freehold forty-shilling franchise for knights of shires
rubrics_metrics.description: Knights of the shires shall be chosen of people dwelling in the same counties; every man shall have freehold to the value of forty shillings by the year within the county (clear of charges except parliamentary and parochial taxes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory historic property qualification intended to ensure independent freeholders; contextualized by change in money value over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum age of voter (21)
rubrics_metrics.description: No person under twenty one years of age shall be capable of voting for any member.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to all sorts of members (boroughs and counties).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disqualification for perjury/subornation of perjury
rubrics_metrics.description: No person convicted of perjury, or subornation of perjury, shall be capable of voting in any election.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrity-based disqualification to protect electoral probity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fraudulent freehold grants void for qualification
rubrics_metrics.description: No person shall vote in right of any freehold granted to him fraudulently to qualify him to vote; such fraudulent grants (agreements to reconvey or to defeat the estate) are void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provision to prevent creation of sham freeholds to manufacture votes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twelve months actual possession requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Every voter shall have been in the actual possession, or receipt of the profits, of his freehold to his own use for twelve calendar months before; except it came by descent, marriage, marriage settlement, will, or promotion to a benefice or office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temporal possession requirement to bar recent artificial qualifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annuity/rentcharge registration 12 months rule
rubrics_metrics.description: No person shall vote in respect of an annuity or rentcharge, unless registered with the clerk of the peace twelve calendar months before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registration requirement for such interests to qualify for the franchise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vote in mortgaged or trust-estates determined by possession
rubrics_metrics.description: In mortgaged or trust-estates, the person in possession, under the abovementioned restrictions, shall have the vote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possession, not merely legal title, governs franchise in these cases subject to temporal and other statutory limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: One vote per house or tenement rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Only one person shall be admitted to vote for any one house or tenement, to prevent the splitting of freeholds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevents artificial division of property to multiply votes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Land tax assessment 12-month qualification
rubrics_metrics.description: No estate shall qualify a voter, unless the estate has been assessed to some land tax aid, at least twelve months before the election.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fiscal assessment requirement to prevent recent contrivances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyhold tenants excluded from county freehold franchise
rubrics_metrics.description: No tenant by copy of court roll shall be permitted to vote as a freeholder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical distinction reflecting status of copyholders at the time of the statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Borough franchise varies by charter/custom; statutory limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The right of election in boroughs depends entirely on the several charters, customs, and constitutions of the respective places; statutes (e.g., 2 Geo. II. c. 24) provide that the right shall be allowed according to the last determination of the house of commons concerning it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local variation subject to parliamentary determination; stability enhanced by statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Borough freemen twelve-month freedom rule (3 Geo. III. c. 15)
rubrics_metrics.description: No freeman of any city or borough (other than such as claim by birth, marriage, or servitude) shall be intitled to vote therein unless he hath been admitted to his freedom twelve calendar months before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temporal qualification to prevent recent admissions being used to influence elections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disqualifications for being elected: aliens and minors
rubrics_metrics.description: Those elected must not be aliens born, or minors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Basic capacity limits for eligibility to sit as members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disqualification for certain offices and attainder
rubrics_metrics.description: Those elected must not be any of the twelve judges, nor of the clergy, nor persons attainted of treason or felony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separation of seats (judges sit in lords, clergy in convocation) and fitness based on criminal status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Returning officers (sheriffs, mayors, bailiffs) ineligibility in jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Sheriffs of counties, and mayors and bailiffs of boroughs, are not eligible in their respective jurisdictions as being returning officers; sheriffs of one county are eligible to be knights of another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevents conflict of interest in local returns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Residency/inhabitancy (ideal rule, often disregarded)
rubrics_metrics.description: In strictness, all members ought to be inhabitants of the places for which they are chosen: but this is entirely disregarded in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expresses principle but notes practical departure from it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disqualification: holders/agents of various revenue offices and new crown offices
rubrics_metrics.description: No persons concerned in the management of any duties or taxes created since 1692 (detailed list) nor any persons that hold any new office under the crown created since 1705, are capable of being elected members (with some exceptions like commissioners of the treasury).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory disqualifications intended to prevent crown influence in Commons membership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disqualification: pensioners under the crown
rubrics_metrics.description: No person having a pension under the crown during pleasure, or for any term of years, is capable of being elected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevents crown dependency from creating influence over members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of office under crown vacates seat
rubrics_metrics.description: If any member accepts an office under the crown, except an officer in the army or navy accepting a new commission, his seat is void; but such member is capable of being re-elected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule designed to check executive influence while permitting re-election where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property qualification for members (knights and burgesses)
rubrics_metrics.description: All knights of the shire shall be actual knights or notable esquires and gentlemen with estates sufficient to be knights; ordaining that every knight of a shire shall have a clear estate of freehold or copyhold to the value of six hundred pounds per annum, and every citizen and burgess to the value of three hundred pounds (with exceptions for eldest sons of peers and members for universities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory property qualifications for eligibility, sworn and recorded when taking seat; intended to balance borough and county representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oath and written particulars at taking seat
rubrics_metrics.description: Of this qualification the member must make oath, and give in the particulars in writing, at the time of his taking his seat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure to evidence and enforce the property/qualification requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writ and precept timeline for initiating elections
rubrics_metrics.description: When parliament is summoned the lord chancellor (or speaker by order) sends warrant to the clerk of the crown who issues writs to the sheriff of every county. Within three days after receipt the sheriff must send his precept to returning officers; returning officers must proceed to election within eight days from receipt, giving four days' notice; and return chosen persons with the precept to the sheriff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory timings and chain of process to initiate and conduct elections; noncompliance incurs penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: County (knights of shire) election by sheriff at county court
rubrics_metrics.description: Elections of knights of the shire must be proceeded to by the sheriffs themselves in person, at the next county court that shall happen after the delivery of the writ; if the court day conflicts the sheriff may adjourn and fix a date not longer than sixteen days nor shorter than ten, but cannot alter the place without consent of all candidates; ten days public notice must be given of election time/place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed procedural safeguards to ensure local and public electoral process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of undue influence and military removal
rubrics_metrics.description: All undue influences upon the electors are illegal and strongly prohibited; soldiers quartered in the place must remove at least one day before the election to the distance of two miles or more and not return till one day after the poll is ended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirmed as essential to free elections; tie to Locke's political theory on corruption of representative processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Riots and interference voiding elections; prohibited recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: Riots have been frequently determined to make an election void. By vote of the house of commons no lord of parliament, or lord lieutenant of a county, has any right to interfere in the election of commoners; and by statute the lord warden of the cinque ports shall not recommend any members there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanisms to shield elections from aristocratic and executive interference; statutory and parliamentary controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalties for revenue officers interfering in elections
rubrics_metrics.description: If any officer of the excise, customs, stamps, or certain other branches of the revenue intermeddles in elections by persuading or dissuading any voter, he forfeits 100_l and is disabled to hold any office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory financial and disability penalties to deter administrative meddling in elections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bribery prohibitions and penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: No candidate shall, after the date (teste) of the writs, or after the vacancy, give any money or entertainment to his electors, or promise to give any, either to particular persons, or to the place in general, to influence being elected; on pain of being incapable to serve for that place. If any money, gift, office, employment, or reward be given or promised to any voter to influence him, both giver and taker forfeit 500_l and are forever disabled from voting and holding any office in any corporation, unless before conviction he discovers another offender and is indemnified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strict anti-bribery statute with large forfeitures and lifelong disabilities, but with conditional indemnity for an informer before conviction; historical precedents and enforcement concerns noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Returning officer and candidate oaths against bribery
rubrics_metrics.description: The returning officer first takes an oath against bribery and for the due execution of his office; candidates, if required, must swear to their qualification; and electors in counties are compellable to take the oath of abjuration and that against bribery and corruption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oath-taking framed as an additional safeguard; author suggests elected members should also be bound by the anti-bribery oath.

rubrics_metrics.name: Returning and transmission of election returns; penalties for false returns
rubrics_metrics.description: Returning officer in boroughs returns his precept to the sheriff with persons elected; the sheriff returns the whole to the clerk of the crown before meeting or within 14 days for occasional vacancies, under penalty of 500_l. If sheriff does not return knights duly elected he forfeits 100_l; returning officer in boroughs for false return 40_l; they are also liable to action with double damages by later statutes; any person bribing returning officer forfeits 300_l.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple statutory penalties to ensure accuracy and honesty of returns and to deter bribery of officers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Members returned sit until house adjudges return illegal
rubrics_metrics.description: The members returned by the returning officer are the sitting members, until the house of commons, upon petition, shall adjudge the return to be false and illegal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internal parliamentary control (petitions) is the mechanism for disputing returns rather than external automatic disqualification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speakers and their differing roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Each house has its speaker. The speaker of the house of lords is the lord chancellor (keeper of the great seal) and may give opinion and argue questions. The speaker of the house of commons is chosen by the house but must be approved by the king and cannot give his opinion or argue any question in the house.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different functional norms for presiding officers in the two houses reflecting constitutional roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Majority rule and open voting
rubrics_metrics.description: In each house the act of the majority binds the whole; this majority is declared by votes openly and publicly given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open voting is preferred in Commons as members are accountable to constituents; secret ballot seen as unsuitable to parliamentary accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for private vs public bills (petition vs motion)
rubrics_metrics.description: To bring a private bill a petition must be presented by a member (setting forth the grievance); petitions founded on disputed facts are referred to a committee, which examines and reports before leave to bring in the bill. Public matters: the bill is brought in upon motion made to the house without a petition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiates intake processes for private relief and public legislation; judicial examination for contested factual bases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and drafting of bills (skeleton with blanks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons directed to bring in a bill present it drawn on paper with many blanks or void spaces where anything occurs that is dubious or necessary to be settled by parliament (e.g., precise dates, nature and quantity of penalties, sums of money).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bills initially function as skeletal instruments to be filled by parliamentary decision; in Lords private bills perused by two judges for legal propriety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three readings, committee stage and committee of the whole
rubrics_metrics.description: Bill is read first and second (speaker opens substance and puts question), after second reading it is committed (either to a selected committee or to a committee of the whole house). In committee the bill is debated clause by clause, amendments made, blanks filled; chairman reports amendments; house reconsiders; after concurrence the bill is engrossed and read a third time, with possible further amendments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard multi-stage parliamentary processing with clause-by-clause scrutiny in committee and formal engrossing before final passage in each house.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engrossing, ryder and transmission between houses
rubrics_metrics.description: After committee and reconsideration the bill is ordered to be engrossed on parchment; if a new clause is added at a late stage a separate piece of parchment (a ryder) is tacked on. Member carries the bill to the other house for concurrence; if amendments are made they are sent back and resolved through conference or dropped if irreconcilable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural devices to record final text and to manage inter-house amendment disputes, including conferences of nominated members to settle differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royal assent modes and formulae (in person or by letters patent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Royal assent is given either in person when king comes to house of peers (titles of bills read and clerk declares the king's answer in Norman-French: 'le roy le veut' or 'soit fait come il est desire', or 'le roy s'avisera' if he refuses), or by statute (33 Hen. VIII c. 21) by letters patent under the great seal signed and notified in his absence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only upon royal assent does a bill become a statute or act of parliament; practice preserves historical formulae and ceremonial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statute publication and permanence
rubrics_metrics.description: An act of parliament, once assented to, is placed among the records of the kingdom and binds every subject and dominion; no formal promulgation is necessary though copies are usually printed; formerly sheriffs proclaimed statutes locally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statute is highest earthly authority; alteration, dispensation, suspension, or repeal requires same forms and authority of parliament; royal dispensing without parliament declared illegal (1 W. & M. st. 2. c. 2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjournment vs prorogation vs dissolution
rubrics_metrics.description: An adjournment is a continuance of the session from one day to another by authority of each house separately; prorogation is the continuance of parliament from one session to another and puts an end to the session (unfinished bills must be resumed de novo); dissolution is distinct (not detailed in this chunk).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjournment preserves state of business; prorogation ends session with different procedural consequences; the king may signify pleasure leading houses to adjourn or face prorogation.
